title: 'Dixieland' versus jazz and ragtime; sharing sheet music
summary: New Orleans bought music from St. Louis publishers, and downtown bands pooled money and exchanged books.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: They're not, it's too many notes, and that goes for some of your trumpet players too, playing, playing what they call, what is it, jazz music. See, there's no such thing as Dix-Line music, it's jazz music, that's what we play. Ragtime music, see? Because that's the first music we played, Ragtime music. Now St. Louis should have had credit for Ragtime music. They should have, because we bought all our music from St. Louis, but we paid away from them. See? New Orleans played the music. But St. Louis, well we bought the music, Scott Johnson, Walter Jacobs and Tom Tanker, and we bought all our music from those guys. See? But then they had no bands up there playing that music, see? See?

See? That's why I said they should have got the credit, but we beat them to the punch. Because we used to buy, because five, six guys in the band, seven guys in a string band was a big band. Everyone in that band would join that club for a dollar a month, didn't we? Right. Yeah. Like you get two of the same numbers, you get two numbers of the same numbers, we ain't got to trade with you for one of the, see? See? See? Bands got along, see? You had to go somewhere and play some quadrules or know something you had to play. You didn't have it, you could borrow the music from the other band. Borrow his book. He'd play there and leave his book and pass by and pick up the book. See? Nobody was going to take none of your music. Because they all had the music. That was the downtown bands. Not the uptown bands, see? Because they had a few good bands, they had a band uptown, they called Olivia's Band, but I didn't know too much about that band. Charlie Olivia. Yeah. I didn't know too much about that band. And I'll tell you another trumpet player was up there, Edward Klim. I don't know.
